question: New sub starts Monday and HMRC verification came back saying he's registered to be paid net. How much do I hold back off his invoices?
reference_answer: A registered sub you can verify gets the standard rate, which is 20%. You only take it from the labour part of the invoice: VAT, materials he bought himself, consumables, plant he hired and fuel (not travel fuel) come off first. You pay the 20% over to HMRC; it counts towards his own tax and NI.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.12 How to calculate the amount to deduct

question: Tried to verify a plasterer, he gave me his UTR but under his trading name and HMRC came back unmatched. What rate do I use and what goes on his statement?
reference_answer: If HMRC cannot match the sub, they tell you to deduct at the higher rate, 30%. The deduction statement must then show the verification reference HMRC gave you for the higher-rate deduction. A trading name isn't a legal identity, so ask him for the legal name, UTR and NI number exactly as registered and verify again; if it then matches, use the rate HMRC gives.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 6.3 Use of trading names
hmrc-cis-340 section 3.15 Providing documentary evidence of a deduction

question: We last used a bricklayer in March 2024 and want him back now. Surely I don't have to verify him again, he's been on our books before?
reference_answer: You can skip verification only if he was on one of your CIS returns in this tax year or the two before it. We are now in 2026-27, so the window goes back to 6 April 2024. March 2024 falls in the 2023-24 tax year, so he is outside the window and you must verify him again before paying.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.2 When a contractor has to verify a subcontractor

question: Groundworker we paid gross in July 2025 is back on site. Do I need to re-verify, and do I keep paying him gross?
reference_answer: No new verification is needed: July 2025 is in the 2025-26 tax year, which is inside the current-plus-two-previous-years window. You pay him the same way as last time, so gross, unless HMRC has written to say his status changed. You are allowed to assume the status you were last told still holds.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.2 When a contractor has to verify a subcontractor
hmrc-cis-340 section 3.3 Paying the subcontractor gross or under deduction

question: Our sister company in our group used this electrician last year. Can we pay him without verifying ourselves?
reference_answer: Yes, if the other company is in our group and verified him or put him on a CIS return this tax year or in the last two. For CIS, companies are in a group when one owns at least 75% of the other, or a third company owns at least 75% of both. Otherwise you verify him as normal.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.4 Companies within a group

question: Can I verify a sub with HMRC before we've agreed anything, just to know his deduction rate while I'm pricing the job?
reference_answer: No. The regulations only let a contractor verify once you have an agreed contract with him, or once you have formally accepted his tender. Price the job first, agree or accept, then verify before the first payment.

question: Tiler, not VAT registered, invoices us £1,000: £600 labour and £400 for tiles he bought, and the £400 includes the VAT he paid at the merchant. What's the CIS deduction and what do I pay him?
reference_answer: Because he is not VAT registered, the VAT he paid on the tiles counts as part of his materials cost. Take the £400 off, leaving £600 subject to CIS. 20% of that is £120, so you pay him £880 and put total £1,000, materials £400 and deduction £120 on your return. Keep evidence of what he paid for the tiles.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.12 How to calculate the amount to deduct

question: VAT-registered painter sends £2,000 labour plus £500 paint plus 20% VAT on top. Do I take the 20% CIS off the VAT as well? And should he even be charging us VAT?
reference_answer: CIS is never taken from VAT, and for a VAT-registered sub the materials figure is also net of VAT. So the deduction is 20% of the £2,000 labour, which is £400. On the VAT: if you are both VAT registered and the payment is reported under CIS, painting is a specified service and the domestic reverse charge applies, so he should not charge you VAT; you account for it on your own return instead (unless you are an end user and told him so in writing).
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.12 How to calculate the amount to deduct
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: How the reverse charge works'

question: Our groundworker owns his own mini digger and wants to put 'plant hire' on his invoice so less CIS gets taken. Is that allowed?
reference_answer: No. Plant hire can be treated like materials only when the sub actually hired it from someone else. For plant he owns there is no notional hire charge to deduct, although fuel the digger burns can still count as materials. Check with him and keep records, or you may be liable for the under-deduction.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.14 Plant hire claimed as materials

question: A sub has added £80 of diesel for driving to site and £120 for digs on his invoice. Do those come off before I work out the 20%?
reference_answer: No. Travel costs, including fuel for getting to site, and subsistence such as accommodation are part of the gross payment and the deduction is taken from them too. Only fuel used in the work itself (not for travelling), materials, consumables, hired plant and prefabrication come off before the 20%.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.11 Making a payment under deduction
govuk-cis-contractor 'How to make a CIS deduction'

question: We held back £400 from a £2,000 invoice because the sub's work wasn't up to standard. Is the CIS worked out on £2,000 or £1,600?
reference_answer: Money you withhold because you believe the sub breached the contract is a set-off, and a set-off reduces the payment. So you take the 20% from £1,600 and show £1,600 as the gross payment on the monthly return. This is different from a contra charge (goods or services you supplied to him), which does not reduce the CIS figure.

question: Releasing a 5% retention now on a job finished two years ago. Since then the sub has got gross payment status. Do I deduct from the retention or not?
reference_answer: Retentions follow the normal rules, and what matters is the sub's status on the day you pay, not the date of the work. Before releasing it, decide whether you need to verify him again (were you including him on returns in the current or last two tax years?). If HMRC confirms gross status, pay the retention gross.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.2 When a contractor has to verify a subcontractor

question: For the tax month ending 5 December, when does the CIS return have to reach HMRC and when do I have to pay the deductions over if I pay by bank transfer?
reference_answer: The return must reach HMRC by 19 December, 14 days after the tax month closes. Deductions paid electronically are due within 17 days, so by 22 December (19 December if paying by post or cheque); if the 22nd falls on a weekend or holiday, pay by the banking day before. You owe the amount you should have deducted even if you forgot to deduct it.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 4.12 Making payments to HMRC

question: We didn't pay a single sub in October. Do I still have to send HMRC anything?
reference_answer: Yes. Since 6 April 2026 a mainstream contractor that has paid subs before must file a nil return by the 19th if it paid nobody in the tax month. The only way out is to tell HMRC in advance that you will pay no subs, at least 14 days before that tax month starts (an inactivity notice, lasting at most 6 months). If you do neither you get a late filing penalty.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 4.5 No return due for the month
hmrc-cis-340 section 4.18 Penalties for late monthly returns

question: We missed taking CIS off one sub for three months, honest mistake. HMRC say we owe the 20% ourselves. Is there any way out of paying it?
reference_answer: The contractor is liable for deductions it should have made, but HMRC can direct that you don't pay the shortfall. You need to show you took reasonable care and the miss was a good-faith error (or you genuinely thought CIS did not apply), or that the sub was not taxable on the money or has declared it and paid his tax. If HMRC refuses, you can appeal within 30 days after HMRC's refusal.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 4.12 Making payments to HMRC

question: We're a limited company and the main contractors take 20% off us. How do we get that money back?
topic: CIS set-off for limited company subcontractors
reference_answer: A company sets the CIS taken from it against what it owes HMRC (monthly or quarterly) in PAYE, NI, student loans and CIS deducted from its own subs, and shows this on the EPS. Any surplus is carried forward within the same tax year. After the year end, once the final FPS and EPS are in, leftover deductions can be repaid or used against the company's Corporation Tax. Keep records of the set-off (form CIS132 can be used).
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 1.11 Subcontractors setting off deductions

question: Can we just put the CIS that main contractors took off us on the company's Corporation Tax return and claim it back that way?
topic: CIS set-off for limited company subcontractors
reference_answer: No. A limited company should not use its Corporation Tax return to claim its CIS deductions and risks a penalty for doing so. The deductions go through the payroll scheme: set them off on the EPS against PAYE, NI and CIS you owe, carry any surplus forward in the year, and claim a refund after the year end.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 1.11 Subcontractors setting off deductions

question: We're a company with two directors and want gross payment status. What turnover do we need to show?
reference_answer: HMRC looks at construction turnover for the past year, leaving out VAT and materials. A company needs £30,000 per director or £100,000 across the company; a company run by five or fewer people needs £30,000 per person. You also have to pass the business test (you do building work in the UK and the money goes through a bank account) and show your tax and NI have been paid on time.
cited_clauses: govuk-cis-subcontractor 'How to get gross payment status'
cis-regs-2005 regulation 27 Evidence prescribed to satisfy the business test

question: HMRC letter says we're failing the annual gross status review. How long have we got, can we appeal, and if we lose it when can we reapply?
reference_answer: You can first write back explaining why; if HMRC accepts it you keep the status. If not, they write again and the status goes 90 days later; you can appeal within 30 days of that letter, and an appeal holds off the cancellation until it is decided. After a normal cancellation you must wait one year to reapply. If it is cancelled straight away for false information, fraud or knowing failures (including the 2026 supply-chain fraud rules), the wait is five years.

question: Heard that since April 2026 HMRC can make us pay if some sub-sub further down our chain dodges CIS or PAYE. Is that right, and how bad can it get?
reference_answer: Yes. From 6 April 2026, if you paid a sub and knew, or ought to have known, that someone in the chain on the same work was deliberately not deducting or paying over CIS or PAYE, HMRC can make you liable for a sum matching 20% of what you paid. A penalty of up to 30% of that amount can follow, and part or all of a company's penalty can be passed to a director whose actions caused it. Your gross status can also be cancelled with immediate effect, with a five-year bar on reapplying.

question: What actually changed in CIS from 6 April 2026? Give me the list for the office.
reference_answer: Three things. Mainstream contractors must again file a nil return for months with no sub payments, unless they told HMRC in advance. Money paid to councils and listed public bodies are no longer contract payments, so no verifying, deducting or reporting them. And new anti-fraud rules apply: liability where you knew, or ought to have known, about deliberate non-compliance in the chain, penalties up to 30%, immediate loss of gross status and a five-year wait to reapply.

question: The HMRC simplification note calls the new public bodies rule regulation 24ZA, but our CIS software says it's 23A. Which is right?
reference_answer: The made regulations (SI 2026/289, in force 6 April 2026) put the rule in as regulation 23A of the 2005 CIS Regulations. The January 2026 draft for consultation numbered it 24ZA, and the policy paper kept that number. The wording is the same: paying a body listed in section 59(1), paragraphs (b) to (k), falls outside the meaning of contract payment.

question: We've paid the county council's highways team to do the road crossing into our site. I need to verify them and take 20% like any other sub, yes?
reference_answer: No. Since 6 April 2026 a payment to a local authority or one of the listed public bodies no longer counts as a contract payment. You should not verify them, should not deduct anything, and should not put the payment on your monthly return.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 2.11 Local authorities and public bodies as subcontractors

question: Do I need to take the 20% CIS off the carpet fitter's invoice on the show flat?
reference_answer: No. Carpet fitting is one of the jobs outside CIS, so you pay the carpet fitter without a deduction. Vinyl, lino or laminate floors fitted to finish a building are inside the scheme.
cited_clauses: govuk-cis-contractor 'Construction work not covered by CIS'
hmrc-cis-340 Appendix C, C.3 Finishing operations

question: We hire scaffolding from a firm that just drops it off, and on another job a scaffolder erects it. Which one is CIS?
reference_answer: Hiring scaffolding with no labour is outside CIS. Putting up and taking down scaffolding is a construction operation, so payments to the scaffolder fall inside the scheme.
cited_clauses: govuk-cis-contractor 'Construction work not covered by CIS'

question: A labour agency sends us three labourers paid on timesheets at a day rate. Do we run CIS on the agency's invoices, and should they be reverse charging the VAT?
topic: CIS and reverse charge for labour agencies
reference_answer: If the workers do construction work under their contracts with the agency, it counts as your subcontractor and you apply CIS when you pay it; but if IR35 (off-payroll) rules cover the engagement, the payment is not a contract payment. For VAT, an employment business supplying workers (timesheets, hourly or daily rates, you direct the work) is supplying staff, not construction services, so there is no reverse charge and it charges VAT normally. A labour-only subcontractor that prices and is responsible for the work is different and is reverse charged.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 2.13 Rules for agency workers
hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Supplies of labour vs supplies of staff'

question: Our client is a property investment company, not a builder, but it's spent about £3.5m on refurbs this year on flats it lets out. Should they be taking CIS off our payments?
reference_answer: Probably yes. A business outside construction becomes a deemed contractor once its construction spend goes over £3 million in a rolling 12 months. The own-property exemption only covers buildings used for its own business; property held for letting or as an investment does not qualify, so payments for that work are inside CIS.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 2.5 Expenditure incurred by certain businesses on their own property

question: Sub's invoice for first-fix plumbing on a shop fit-out has 20% VAT on it. We're both VAT registered, he's on CIS, and we bill the shop owner. Should it have been reverse charge?
reference_answer: Yes. Installing plumbing is a specified service, you are both VAT registered and you report his payment under CIS, and you aren't the end user, because you supply the work on to your client. Ask him for a corrected invoice marked as reverse charge. Even with the wrong invoice, it is your job to self-account for the VAT on your return.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Services covered and not covered by the construction reverse charge'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: End users and intermediary suppliers: End users'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: Invoices: Invoices'

question: Our roofer has gross payment status, so there's no reverse charge on his invoices, right?
reference_answer: Wrong. The supplier's CIS payment status makes no difference to the VAT reverse charge. If you are both VAT registered, the payment is reported under CIS and the work is a specified service, the reverse charge applies whether he is paid gross or under deduction.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: Who needs to apply the construction reverse charge: Gross Payment subcontractors'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: Who needs to apply the construction reverse charge: Description of roles'

question: Housing association client says they're an 'end user' so we should charge them normal VAT. What do we need from them before we stop reverse charging?
reference_answer: The end user exception only works if the customer confirms it to you in writing, no later than the supply or in the written contract. A letter, email or a clause in the contract will do; keep a copy to show HMRC. Once you have it, charge VAT as normal. Without written notice you should keep applying the reverse charge.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: End users and intermediary suppliers: End user notification'
hmrc-vatrevcon 'How the construction reverse charge works: End users and intermediary suppliers: End users'

question: Job is mostly fitting CCTV and alarms, but our sub also digs the trenches and puts in the concrete posts. Reverse charge or not?
reference_answer: Installing security systems on its own is outside the reverse charge. But if it is one supply together with specified services such as groundworks, the whole supply is reverse charged. If the specified part is no more than 5% of what the contract is worth, both sides can agree at the start to disregard it; that is optional and is not worked out invoice by invoice.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Supplies where the reverse charge element is a minor part'

question: We're building new houses for sale. Does our groundworker have to reverse charge us?
topic: VAT reverse charge and zero-rated new build
reference_answer: No. Groundworks done in the course of building new dwellings are normally zero-rated, and zero-rated supplies are outside the reverse charge because there's no VAT to shift onto you. It only covers standard-rated and reduced-rated services.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Zero-rated supplies'
vat-notice-708 paragraph 3.3.4 Work closely connected to the construction of the building

question: We knocked down a bungalow to ground level and are building a new detached house on the plot for the owner. Zero-rated or 5%?
reference_answer: It can be zero-rated. A building put up after the old one is flattened right down to ground level counts as a new qualifying building if it meets the dwelling tests: self-contained, can be used and sold separately, and built in line with planning consent. Your services must be part of the building works and not be excluded items (for example professional fees or plant hired without an operator).
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 3.4 Services excluded from zero rating

question: Building a granny annexe at the back of the client's garden. It can't be sold separately from the main house. That's zero-rated new build, isn't it?
reference_answer: No. An annexe that can't be lived in or sold on its own, apart from the main house, does not meet the 'designed as a dwelling' conditions, so building it can't take the zero rate; expect 20%.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 3.2.2 Examples of when a qualifying building is not constructed

question: Renovating a terraced house that's been empty for three years. Can we charge 5% VAT, and what proof do we need?
reference_answer: Yes, renovating a home nobody has occupied for at least 2 years before you start can be charged at 5%. Proof can come from electoral roll or council tax records, utility companies or the council's Empty Property Officer; a letter from that officer is enough on its own. Some items stay at 20%: carpets, fitted wardrobes, scaffolding, hire of goods, landscaping and professional fees.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 8.3.2 Proof that the premises has been empty for 2 years

question: The new owner moved into the empty house a few weeks before we started the refurb. Can we still do it at 5%?
reference_answer: Normally, if the house is lived in when the work starts, it is standard-rated. There is an exception for a single household dwelling: 5% can still apply if it stood empty for two years before the purchase, no renovation was done in that period, you supply the work to the owner directly, and the work is within a year of the purchase. A subcontractor on that job must charge 20%.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 8.3.4 People living in the premises whilst you carry out the work

question: Converting an old office block into four flats for a developer. What VAT rate do we charge?
reference_answer: Turning offices or other non-residential premises into homes, or altering how many dwellings there are, is a qualifying conversion at 5% for a normal developer. It would be 0% only if the conversion were done for a relevant housing association. Fitting non-building-material goods such as carpets stays at 20%, and work unrelated to the conversion cannot be reduced-rated.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 7.3 Conversions into single household dwellings

question: We're a sub on a new care home. The client gave the main contractor a zero-rating certificate. Can we zero-rate our invoices to the main contractor too?
reference_answer: No. A subcontractor working for a main contractor should not be given the certificate and must charge standard rate on work for a certificated building such as a relevant residential building. Only the main contractor's supply to the client may be zero-rated using the certificate.

question: Fitting kitchens in new-build flats including fridge-freezers and dishwashers. Is everything zero-rated?
reference_answer: Not everything. On a zero-rated new build, building materials you fit take the zero rate, and kitchen units are ordinarily fitted items. Fridges, freezers, dishwashers and similar appliances are not building materials, so the goods are standard-rated, though your fitting labour on a 0% project may stay at 0%. A cooker only counts as a building material if it is made to warm the room or the water.
cited_clauses: vat-notice-708 paragraph 11.2 Goods 'incorporated' by a builder
vat-notice-708 paragraph 13.6 Electrical and gas appliances
vat-notice-708 paragraph 13.9 Examples of articles not ordinarily incorporated in dwellings

question: Our sub-contract has no payment terms written in at all. When do interim payments fall due and when is the final date to pay?
reference_answer: Where the contract is silent, the statutory Scheme fills the gap (England and Wales). For a job of 45 days or more, interim payments are due on the later of 7 days after the end of each period (28 days if none is set) or the payee's claim, and the final date to pay is 17 days after the due date. The final payment falls due 30 days after completion or the claim, if later. The payer must also issue a payment notice within 5 days of each due date.
cited_clauses: scheme-cc-1998 Schedule Part II paragraphs 2, 4 and 5
scheme-cc-1998 Schedule Part II paragraph 12 'relevant period'

question: We want to pay a sub less than his application because of defects. Contract doesn't say anything about pay less notices. What's my deadline?
reference_answer: A pay less notice has to say the sum you consider due and how you worked it out. Where the contract sets no period, it must reach the sub at least 7 days ahead of the final date to pay. Miss it and you owe the full notified sum.

question: The main contractor never sent a payment notice within 5 days of the due date and now isn't paying us. What can we do?
reference_answer: If the payer misses its payment notice, you can serve your own notice stating the sum due and how it is calculated at any time afterwards; the final date to pay moves back by the number of days you were late. If your contract let you send an application before the due date and you did, that application already counts as your notice. The payer must then pay the notified sum by the final date unless it serves a valid pay less notice.

question: Our sub-contract says we only pay the sub once the client pays us. Client hasn't paid, so we don't have to pay the sub yet, correct?
reference_answer: No. A clause making payment depend on you being paid by someone else has no effect unless the third party (or someone up the chain) is insolvent. With the clause struck out, the parties can agree other terms, and otherwise the Scheme's payment provisions apply, so payment is due on the normal dates.

question: Main contractor is way past the final date and hasn't paid. Can we down tools, and what notice do we have to give?
reference_answer: Yes, if the notified sum is not paid by the final date you can suspend some or all of your work. You must first give at least 7 days' written notice saying you intend to suspend and why. The right ends when you are paid in full; the other side must pay your reasonable costs of suspending, and the suspension period is added to your time to finish.

question: If we go to adjudication over an unpaid valuation, how long does it all take?
reference_answer: After you give notice of adjudication, the adjudicator should be appointed and the dispute referred within 7 days. The decision is due within 28 days of the referral; this can go to 42 days if the referring party agrees, or longer if both sides agree. The decision binds both sides until the dispute is settled by court, arbitration or agreement.

question: The job was only four weeks long, so the sub can't take us to adjudication, can he?
reference_answer: He can. The 45-day point only decides whether a party is entitled to stage payments. The right to adjudicate applies to any construction contract, however short (contracts with a homeowner living in the property are excluded from the Act).

question: District council job, estimated £180k of works. Their tender pack wants three years of audited accounts and a pre-qualification questionnaire before we can even bid. Are they allowed to do that?
reference_answer: For a regulated contract under the threshold, a council inviting tenders cannot filter bidders through a separate suitability stage such as financial or technical checks. That ban lifts for works contracts at or above £207,720 for councils (£135,018 for central government), so a £180k works job is caught. The council can still look at suitability when it assesses tenders. The ban does not apply to call-offs under a framework or to Welsh devolved authorities.

question: Council in England is tendering a £1.2m school refurb. Is that a full Procurement Act contract or a below-threshold one, and what does that mean for us?
reference_answer: Since 1 January 2026 the works threshold is £5,193,000, so £1.2m falls below the threshold and the lighter Part 6 rules apply. Because it is above £207,720, the council may run a separate suitability check ahead of tenders. If it advertises the work, a tender notice for below-threshold work has to go on Find a Tender first, and a contract details notice has to follow the award.

question: Council's got a £25k repair job. Will it show up on Find a Tender, or do they just ring round?
reference_answer: For councils (not central government), a below-threshold contract only becomes notifiable at £30,000 including VAT. Below that nothing requires a tender notice or contract details notice, and the council can ask targeted suppliers for quotes. If it does advertise a notifiable contract, the tender notice has to appear on Find a Tender before anywhere else.

question: Can our local council keep a small works tender just for local firms? We'd love that.
reference_answer: Yes, in England since the 2026 Order, councils and parish councils may reserve below-threshold competitions to suppliers based in the UK or in a local area. 'Local' means the council's own area, optionally with neighbouring counties or London boroughs, and this has to be spelled out in the tender notice or advert. 'Based in' means having substantive operations there, whoever owns you. They can also reserve competitions to SMEs. Central government bodies follow a separate policy.

question: How fast does the council legally have to pay our invoices on a below-threshold works contract?
reference_answer: Within 30 days, starting on the day they receive the invoice or, if later, the day it falls due under the invoice. That does not apply if they treat the invoice as invalid or dispute it, but they must tell you without undue delay if so. A valid invoice needs the minimum information the Act requires plus anything the contract asks for.

question: We're a sub on a big council contract under the Procurement Act. The main contractor's sub-contract says they pay us in 60 days. Can they do that?
reference_answer: Not if the council's contract counts as a public contract. The Act implies the 30-day payment terms into all public sub-contracts (one substantially for performing the public contract), and any term trying to override them has no effect, so 60 days cannot be enforced. Paying earlier than 30 days is allowed. This does not apply to sub-contracts under concession contracts, private utility contracts or school contracts.

question: Council always pays us late. Is there anywhere I can see how quickly they actually pay?
reference_answer: Authorities have to publish their payments compliance notices on Find a Tender no more than 30 days after each six-month reporting period (periods run from 1 October and 1 April). It shows their average days to pay, the share paid within 30, 31 to 60 and 61+ days, and the share paid on 30-day terms. It is only required for public contracts; including below-threshold contracts is voluntary.

question: Thresholds changed in January 2026, but the council published the tender notice for our job in December 2025. Which thresholds apply?
reference_answer: The old ones. The new thresholds from 1 January 2026 do not affect a procurement that had already started, and publishing a tender notice before that date counts as starting it.

question: What exactly counts as an SME when councils reserve tenders for small firms? We've got 30 staff and £6m turnover.
reference_answer: Under the Procurement Act an SME has under 250 staff, and either turnover of £44 million or less or a balance sheet of £38 million or less. With 30 staff and £6m turnover you are an SME.

question: If we bid for a central government job worth over £5m a year, what do they want to see about how we pay our own subbies?
reference_answer: Since September 2019 bidders for central government contracts over £5 million a year must show they have effective payment systems. The standard is that 95% of supply chain invoices are paid within 60 days, and firms that miss it could be stopped from winning government work.

question: Last year a council terminated one of our contracts for poor performance. Could that get us excluded from future public tenders?
reference_answer: It can. Breaching a contract with a public body in a sufficiently serious way is a discretionary exclusion ground, and termination (or part termination), damages or a settlement count as serious. Failing to perform to the authority's standard after a proper chance to improve is also a ground. Discretionary means the buyer decides whether to exclude.

question: We've never bid for public work. How do we get set up to see and bid for council tenders?
topic: Registering on the central digital platform
reference_answer: Register on Find a Tender, the government's central digital platform, which is free. Create a One Login account on GOV.UK, register your organisation as a supplier with your Companies House number (or get a platform identifier), and complete your supplier information such as connected persons, exclusions and financial details. Share your unique identifier with the buyer before award, and set up saved searches to get emailed about new tenders.
cited_clauses: procurement-supplier-guide 'How to register your organisation and find your unique identifier'
procurement-supplier-guide 'Searching for opportunities and setting up notifications'

question: What do I take off this new lad's money?
reference_answer: It depends on what HMRC says when you verify him, which you must do before the first payment if he is new to you. You need his UTR, his NI number if he is a sole trader (or company details), and his name exactly as registered. The result will be 20% if registered, 30% if not registered or not matched, or nothing if he has gross status, and the deduction only applies to the labour part after his own materials, hired plant and VAT.
cited_clauses: hmrc-cis-340 section 3.12 How to calculate the amount to deduct

question: Is this invoice meant to be reverse charge or not?
reference_answer: Need more detail: what work it is for, whether both firms are VAT registered, whether the payment is reported under CIS, whether the work is zero-rated, and whether the customer has given written end user notice. It covers standard or reduced-rated construction services between VAT-registered businesses reported under CIS. It does not apply to workers supplied by an employment business, zero-rated work, supplies within a VAT group, or customers who have given written end user or intermediary notice.
cited_clauses: hmrc-vatrevcon 'Scope of the construction reverse charge: Background to and relationship to the Construction Industry Scheme (CIS)'

question: What VAT do I put on the house job?
reference_answer: Depends what the job is. Work on existing buildings is usually 20%. A brand new dwelling can be 0%, turning non-residential premises into homes or altering how many dwellings there are is usually 5%, and renovating a home empty for at least 2 years can be 5%. Tell me whether it is new build or existing, how long it has been empty, what the building was before, who the client is and whether you are main contractor or sub.

question: When have I got to pay my sub?
reference_answer: First check what your sub-contract says about due dates and final payment dates; those apply if they are adequate. If the contract is silent, the statutory Scheme sets due dates and a final date to pay 17 days after each due date. If the job is a sub-contract under a Procurement Act public contract, a 30-day maximum from receipt of invoice is implied. Tell me the contract terms and the type of job.
cited_clauses: scheme-cc-1998 Schedule Part II paragraphs 4 and 8

question: Does the council have to put this job out to tender?
reference_answer: It depends on the estimated value, whether it is works or goods and services, whether the buyer is a council or central government, and whether they are using a framework. Below the thresholds (works £5,193,000 from 2026) the council has wide freedom, including asking chosen suppliers for quotes or making a direct award, subject to its own rules. If it advertises a contract worth £30,000 or more, it must first put out a tender notice for below-threshold work.

question: Got a job in Glasgow with no payment terms in the sub-contract. What default periods apply up there?
reference_answer: Not covered. Part II of the Construction Act does reach Scotland, but the default payment rules in our documents are the Scheme for England and Wales only. You would need the Scottish Scheme for Construction Contracts regulations to answer this.

question: What rate of interest can I charge a main contractor who pays us late?
reference_answer: Not covered by these documents. They deal with payment notices, due dates, suspension and adjudication, but not statutory late payment interest. You would need the Late Payment of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 and the current reference rate, or what your contract says.

question: We're bidding for a Welsh council job. What are the procurement thresholds in Wales now?
reference_answer: Not covered. The 2026 threshold changes we have apply to contracts other than those the Welsh Ministers regulate, and say Wales is making its own instrument. You would need the Welsh thresholds regulations or Welsh Government guidance.

question: How do I tell if one of my regular labourers should really be on PAYE instead of CIS? What are the tests?
reference_answer: The documents say you must check whether someone should be an employee and that a wrong status on the return can cost up to £3,000, but they do not set out the status tests. You would need HMRC's employment status guidance (for example the Employment Status Manual or HMRC's status tool).

question: Is there a legal cap on cash retentions? Main contractor wants to hold 10%.
reference_answer: Not covered. Our documents only say how retentions are treated for CIS and VAT, not how much can be held. You would need the contract terms and any specific legislation or guidance on retentions.

question: What's the CITB levy rate this year and when do we pay it?
reference_answer: Not covered. VAT Notice 708 only explains the VAT treatment when a contractor withholds a levy contribution, not the levy rate or payment dates. You would need CITB's own levy guidance and the current Levy Order.

question: Which CIS software is cheapest for a firm with about 20 subbies?
reference_answer: Not covered; the documents do not compare products or prices. They only say you can use HMRC's free CIS online service or commercial CIS software, and that verifying more than 50 subcontractors needs commercial software.

question: When is our company's Corporation Tax due and what's the rate on our profits?
reference_answer: Not covered. The CIS documents only mention Corporation Tax for using leftover CIS deductions after the year end. You would need HMRC's Corporation Tax guidance for rates and payment dates.
